C8.1.q: In mono, you hold one key and press a second. What do you hear?
options: Both notes together, as a chord
Only the first note, as before
Only the second note, which takes over
Nothing until one key is let go
C8.1.why: Mono sounds one note at a time, and the newest key wins.

C8.1.q: In mono, you hold a low key and tap a higher one. What happens when the higher key is let go?
options: The low note comes back by itself
The sound stops until a key is pressed
The higher note keeps on sounding
C8.1.why: In mono, letting go of a key falls back to one that is still held.

C8.1.q: Mono, Legato off, slow Attack. You play overlapping notes. What do you hear?
options: Every note swells in from quiet
One unbroken note with no new swell
Only the first note swells in
C8.1.why: Without legato, each new key starts the envelope again, even when the keys overlap.

C8.1.q: Attack is slow and Legato is on. What do overlapped notes do?
options: Swell in from quiet every time
Stay on the first note's pitch
Change pitch with no new swell
C8.1.why: Legato carries the envelopes on through overlapped notes, so they run together as one unbroken note.

C8.1.q: Legato is on. You want one note in a run to swell in afresh. How do you play it?
options: Press it while the last key is still down
Let go of the last key before pressing it
Hold the last key and tap it several times
Press it together with the last key
C8.1.why: With legato on, separated keys each get their own start, while overlapped keys run together.

C8.1.q: You hold two keys for a chord, but only one note sounds. What do you change?
options: Switch Legato on for the held keys
Turn Envelope 1's Attack up to about 400 ms
Set Voices play back from Mono to poly
Let go of the first key sooner
C8.1.why: Poly sounds every key held, while mono sounds only one note at a time.

C8.2.q: What does Glide do to a new note?
options: Fades its level in slowly from silence
Slides its pitch there from the previous note
Starts the note a little later
Keeps the previous note sounding under it
C8.2.why: Glide makes the pitch travel to the new note from the previous one, over the time you set.

C8.2.q: Glide is about 1 second. You play a low key, then hold one far above. What do you hear?
options: A long, even climb that stops on the note
A quick scoop, then the note at once
A climb that carries on past the note
The high note at once, with no slide
C8.2.why: Glide slides the pitch from the previous note over the set time, and a long time gives a long climb.

C8.2.q: The glide time stays the same. How does a wide jump compare with a narrow one?
options: The wide jump takes longer to arrive
Both move at exactly the same speed
The wide jump does not slide at all
The pitch moves faster over the wide jump
C8.2.why: The time is fixed whatever the distance, so a wide jump has to move faster.

C8.2.q: Glide acts on every note. You play separated low and high keys. What do you hear?
options: Clean jumps, since the keys do not overlap
A slide only when the pitch goes up
A slide on the first note and none after
A scoop into every note from the last one
C8.2.why: Set to every note, glide slides the pitch from the previous note whether or not the keys overlap.

C8.2.q: Glide acts only on overlapped notes. How do you play a clean jump with no slide?
options: Let go of one key before pressing the next
Press the next key while holding the first
Choose a key far from the last one
Hold the new key down for longer
C8.2.why: Only a note pressed while another is still held slides, so separated notes jump cleanly.

C8.2.q: Mono, Legato on, Glide on overlapped notes. What do overlapped notes do?
options: Jump cleanly, and each starts afresh
Slide in pitch, but each starts afresh
Jump cleanly, but run together as one
Slide in pitch and run together as one
C8.2.why: With legato and glide on overlapped notes, overlapped notes slide and run together while separated ones start afresh on their pitch.

C8.3.q: What do the two wheels let you do that envelopes and LFOs do not?
options: Move the sound by hand while a note sounds
Move the sound by themselves on every note
Change the sound only before a note starts
Play more than one note at a time
C8.3.why: Envelopes and LFOs move a sound by themselves, while the wheels let you move it by hand as a note sounds.

C8.3.q: You drag the Bend wheel to the top, then let go. What does the pitch do?
options: It stays up where you left it
It snaps back to the note
It falls the same distance below the note
It carries on rising by itself
C8.3.why: The bend wheel moves pitch by hand and springs back to the middle when you let go.

C8.3.q: Which setting makes the same push of the bend wheel travel further in pitch?
C8.3.why: Bend range says how many semitones the bend wheel reaches at either end.

C8.3.q: You raise the mod wheel halfway and take your hand away. What does the wheel do?
options: Carries on up to the top
C8.3.why: The bend wheel springs back, while the mod wheel stays where you leave it.

C8.3.q: You raise the mod wheel on a held note and nothing at all changes. What is the likely reason?
options: Bend range is set too low
It has sprung back to the middle
It has not been sent anywhere yet
C8.3.why: The mod wheel is a source, so it does nothing until it is sent somewhere.

C8.3.q: The mod wheel is sent to filter cutoff but sits at the bottom. What do you hear?
options: The filter fully open from the start
No change, as none of its amount applies
The filter half open, waiting to move
The pitch pulled down below the note
C8.3.why: The mod wheel is a source, and its position decides how much of its amount is applied.

C8.3.q: The mod wheel is sent to LFO 1 amount. What does raising it do to the note?
options: Bends the pitch steadily upward by itself
Speeds the wobble up without deepening it
Opens the filter as your hand rises
Deepens the wobble by raising the LFO's reach
C8.3.why: Sent to another connection's amount, the wheel fades movement such as vibrato in and out.

CT.1.q: You change only Envelope 1's Attack. Which part of the hit are you shaping?
CT.1.why: A hit has a start, a body and a tail, and Attack is the start.

CT.1.q: Attack goes from 50 ms down to a few milliseconds. How does a bass note change?
options: It strikes where it used to swell in
It drops to a lower pitch
It rings on longer after the key
It stays brighter all the way through
CT.1.why: Attack sets how quickly the note reaches full level, and a few milliseconds turn a swell into a strike.

CT.1.q: Why can a 1 ms Attack add a small click to a note?
options: The pitch starts high and falls quickly
The note is too short to be heard
A level jumping that fast is a sharp edge
The body of the note is missing
CT.1.why: A sudden jump in level is a sharp edge, and a sharp edge contains high frequencies.

CT.1.q: Your bass note starts with a small click on top. Which control do you turn, and which way?
options: Attack, down as far as it goes
Attack, up by a few milliseconds
Sustain, all the way down to 0
CT.1.why: A very fast start adds a click, so a slightly longer Attack keeps the strike but stays clean.

CT.1.q: With Sustain at 0 and a short Decay, why does the Attack setting matter more?
options: The body gets louder than the start
The start is most of what there is
The tail covers up the start
The note no longer has a start
CT.1.why: A hit has a start, a body and a tail, and with a short body the start is most of the sound.

CT.2.q: You strike the low sine before any pitch fall is added. What do you hear?
options: A hard knock, then a low thump
A swoop down from high up
A soft thud with no front to it
A long drum that booms on
CT.2.why: A basic kick needs a fast fall in pitch, and the sine alone is a soft thud with no front.

CT.2.q: Why is the pitch fall in a kick not heard as a melody?
options: It is too quiet under the thump
A sine wave has no pitch to follow
It only happens after the note ends
It is too fast, leaving only a knock
CT.2.why: The pitch falls in a few hundredths of a second, so all it leaves is a knock at the front.

CT.2.q: Why is Osc A pitch, wide the destination used for the kick?
options: It makes the body of the drum last longer
It can move the pitch by as much as four octaves
It keeps the pitch steady on the key played
It turns the sine wave into a brighter shape
CT.2.why: Osc A pitch, wide can move the pitch by as much as four octaves, enough to start the drum high.

CT.2.q: Your kick swoops down like a laser. How do you shrink the swoop to a knock?
options: Lengthen Envelope 1's Decay to about 600 ms
Shorten Envelope 2's Decay and set its Fall to Sharp
Play a lower key so it lands lower
CT.2.why: Envelope 2 on pitch makes the knock, and a short, sharp fall turns the swoop into one.

CT.2.q: The knock of your kick is right, but it should boom for longer. What do you change?
options: Envelope 2's Fall, setting it to Sharp
CT.2.why: Envelope 2 on pitch makes the knock, and Envelope 1 sets the length of the body.

CT.2.q: What does playing a different key do to the kick?
options: Changes the pitch the drum lands on
Changes how long the body lasts
Changes how hard the knock sounds
Changes how fast the pitch falls
CT.2.why: The key you play is the pitch the drum settles on, so each key is a different tuning.

CT.3.q: Which setting decides how far above the note a kick's pitch starts?
CT.3.why: Amount is how far the pitch falls, and Envelope 2's decay is how fast it comes down.

CT.3.q: Your kick's front is a hard knock and you want a soft, round thud. What do you turn?
options: The level of the note, down
CT.3.why: Near and fast is a soft thud, so a smaller Amount softens the front.

CT.3.q: Why does a large, quick fall sound like a hard knock?
options: The body of the kick becomes much louder
The pitch starts much closer to the note
The fall takes much longer to finish
The pitch passes many more frequencies in one instant
CT.3.why: Far and fast gives a hard knock because the pitch crosses many more frequencies in the same instant.

CT.3.q: With a large Amount, you slow Envelope 2's Decay to about 350 ms. What do you get?
options: A soft, round thud with little front
A tick in front of a plain thud
A zap you can follow as a falling note
A hard knock that is almost a click
CT.3.why: A slow fall stops being a knock and is heard as a falling pitch: a zap.

CT.3.q: You take Envelope 2's Decay down to about 10 ms. What happens to the front of the kick?
options: It turns into a zap you can follow
It becomes a harder, longer knock
It stretches into a slow swoop
CT.3.why: Envelope 2's decay is how fast the pitch falls, and at its fastest the front shrinks to a tick.

CT.4.q: How does a sub drop differ from the pitch fall in a kick?
options: It falls over seconds, so the fall is heard
It rises in pitch where a kick falls
It falls faster, so it knocks harder
It keeps a steady pitch as it fades
CT.4.why: A sub drop is the kick idea stretched out: a slow fall in pitch on a low, pure tone.

CT.4.q: Where is a sub drop usually placed?
options: On every beat, in place of the kick
At the very end of each bass note
Under a big hit at the start of a section
Above the melody, high up in pitch
CT.4.why: A sub drop is a slow fall on a low tone, usually placed under a big hit at the start of a section.

CT.4.q: Envelope 2 is sent to pitch but is still short. You hold a low key. What do you hear?
options: A slide down for as long as it sounds
A quick dip at the start of the note
A slow climb up to the note
A steady pitch with no dip at all
CT.4.why: A sub drop needs a slow fall, and a short Envelope 2 gives only a quick dip at the start.

CT.4.q: You want a sub drop to end on a lower pitch. What do you do?
CT.4.why: The key you play is always where the drop lands, and the amount only sets how far above it starts.

CT.4.q: You want a sub drop to start from higher above the note it lands on. What do you change?
options: Hold the key down for longer
CT.4.why: The amount sets how far above the landing note the drop starts.

CT.4.q: How does an Eased fall move compared with a Straight one?
options: At an even pace all the way down
Quickly at first, then lingering near the bottom
Slowly at first, then rushing to the bottom
In small steps, pausing on each one
CT.4.why: A straight fall moves evenly, while an eased fall drops fast and then lingers low.

CT.4.q: You watch the scope while a sub drop slides down. What do the waves do?
options: They get wider as the pitch falls
They get narrower as the pitch falls
They get taller as the pitch falls
They keep the same width throughout
CT.4.why: A sub drop is a slow fall in pitch, and on the scope the waves get wider as it falls.

CT.5.q: How can a bass note get a sharp front without being louder?
options: A long release lets the notes overlap
A filter stays wide open for the whole note
A filter opens briefly at the start, then closes
A high sustain keeps the note at full level
CT.5.why: A fast filter envelope gives every bass note a bright front that closes at once.

CT.5.q: You stretch Envelope 2's Decay on the filter to about 400 ms. What does each note do?
options: Snaps bright, then closes at once
Stays dull and even from start to finish
Says wow as the filter closes slowly
Leaves silence before the next note
CT.5.why: A fast filter envelope gives a bright front, while a slow one closes gradually and says wow.

CT.5.q: Why give Envelope 1 a strong start that settles to a lower level?
options: It stops the notes becoming one drone
It makes every note brighter throughout
It makes the filter close more slowly
It makes each note ring on afterwards
CT.5.why: Envelope 1 shapes the body: a note that strikes and then settles keeps the line from droning.

CT.5.q: A line of short bass notes smears together. Which change separates them?
CT.5.why: A short release leaves a gap of silence before the next note, and the gaps separate the hits.

CT.6.q: What does a small, fast pitch fall add to a bass note?
options: A lower pitch for the whole note
A small knock at the front of the note
A brighter tone while the key is held
A longer tail after the key is let go
CT.6.why: A small, fast pitch fall gives a bass note a front while the note itself stays the same.

CT.6.q: How does the pitch fall on this bass note compare with the one in a kick?
options: The same method, only much smaller
The same size, only much slower
The opposite: it rises where a kick falls
A different method that uses the filter
CT.6.why: It is the kick drum's method at a fraction of the size.

CT.6.q: You raise the Amount to about 60% and the Decay to about 120 ms. What happens?
options: Each note simply begins with no front
Each note has a smaller, tighter knock
Each note swoops in like a laser
Each note settles above the key's pitch
CT.6.why: Small and quick is heard as part of the start, while large or slow is heard as a swoop.

CT.6.q: Your bass notes have started to sound like tom drums. How do you get a defined front back?
options: Make the Amount larger and the Decay quick
Keep the Amount large and slow the Decay
Make the Amount small and the Decay quick
Turn the Amount up and Sustain to 0
CT.6.why: Small and quick reads as attack, while large or slow reads as a swoop.

CT.C.q: In what order is it best to listen to a hidden hit?
options: The body, then the fall, then the start
The fall, then the body, then the start
The body, then the start, then the fall
The start, then the fall, then the body
CT.C.why: Listen to the start first, then the fall, then the body.

CT.C.q: You can follow the target's fall as a falling pitch, but not yours. What does that tell you?
options: The target's fall is faster than yours
The target's fall is slower than yours
The target's body is longer than yours
The target's start is sharper than yours
CT.C.why: A fall you can follow as a pitch is a slow one.

CT.C.q: The target's knock matches yours, but its body lasts longer. Which envelope do you adjust?
options: Envelope 2, which sets the body's length
Envelope 1, which sets the body's length
CT.C.why: The body's length is Envelope 1, and the knock is Envelope 2.

C2.8.q: What does the Peak type do to a sound?
options: Removes a thin slice at the cutoff
Lifts a band around the cutoff and leaves the rest alone
C2.8.why: Peak takes nothing away. It lifts a band around the cutoff and leaves everything else as it was.

C2.8.q: With Peak chosen and Resonance at 0, what do you hear?
C2.8.why: With nothing lifted, Peak changes nothing, so the curve is a flat line.

C2.8.q: How does a Shelf differ from a Low-pass on the top of a sound?
options: A shelf removes the top faster
A shelf turns the top down by a set amount but keeps it
C2.8.why: A low-pass keeps cutting harder the higher you go. A shelf steps down and then stays level.

C2.8.q: On Peak and Shelf, what does the Resonance knob set?
options: How much the band is lifted or the top is turned down
C2.8.why: On both of these types the Resonance knob is the amount.

C2.8.q: You sweep the cutoff with Peak on. What happens to the bass and top?
options: Both stay as loud as before
The bass goes and the top stays
The top goes and the bass stays
C2.8.why: Only the lifted band travels. Peak leaves everything outside it alone.

C2.9.q: Two filters sit one after the other. What do you hear?
C2.9.why: The second filter only gets what the first let through, so each removes more.

C2.9.q: Two filters sit side by side. What do you hear?
options: What passes either filter, added together
C2.9.why: Each filter hears the whole sound and their outputs are added.

C2.9.q: A low-pass at 1.2 kHz followed by a high-pass at 600 Hz leaves what?
options: A band between the two cutoffs
C2.9.why: Each filter takes its own end away, so a band between the cutoffs is left.

C2.9.q: Side by side, a low-pass at 200 Hz and a high-pass at 4 kHz leave what?
options: A narrow band in the middle
Bass and top with the middle scooped out
C2.9.why: One lets the bass through and the other the top, so the middle is missing.

C2.9.q: With those wide-apart cutoffs, you switch to one after the other. Why is it nearly silent?
options: The first keeps only bass and the second then removes the bass
C2.9.why: In a row only what passes both is left, and almost nothing passes both.

C1.10.q: What does giving Osc B more voices with some detune do?
options: Makes it thick and slowly moving
C1.10.why: Several copies slightly apart in pitch drift against one another, which sounds thick and moving.

C1.10.q: B has several voices but Detune is at 0. What happens to the swirl?
options: It stops, because nothing differs in pitch
C1.10.why: The drifting comes from the difference in pitch. With none, nothing drifts.

C1.10.q: What does Osc B's own warp let you do?
options: Reshape B's wave without touching Osc A
C1.10.why: B has its own warp, so its wave is reshaped separately from A's.

C7.7.q: Why does the order of effects matter?
options: Each effect works on what the one before it sends on
Only the first effect is heard
C7.7.why: Each effect receives the output of the one before, so the same settings give different results in a different order.

C7.7.q: Distortion sits after reverb. What happens to the reverb tail?
C7.7.why: The distortion turns up and reshapes the quiet tail as well as the note.

C7.7.q: You want a gritty note with a clean, smooth tail. Which order?
C7.7.why: With distortion first, the reverb echoes an already distorted note and its tail is left alone.

C7.7.q: An EQ cuts the highs before distortion. Why is the sound hardly duller?
options: Distortion makes new high harmonics after the cut
The cut is too small to matter
C7.7.why: The distortion comes after the cut and adds high harmonics of its own.

C7.7.q: Where should an EQ cut go to tame the edge that distortion adds?
C7.7.why: After the distortion, the cut shapes the finished tone, edge included.

C5M.17.q: What do a low-pass and a high-pass in a row leave?
C5M.17.why: Each takes one end away, so the band between the cutoffs is left.

C5M.17.q: How does the Radio macro narrow the band from both ends?
options: One slot moves down and the other up
C5M.17.why: The low-pass comes down while the high-pass comes up, so the edges close in together.

C5M.17.q: Why does this macro sound like the full saw at zero?
options: The filters are switched off by the macro
The saw is louder at zero
C5M.17.why: With both cutoffs at their extremes nothing is removed until the macro turns.

C5M.18.q: Five voices with no detune sound like what?
C5M.18.why: With no difference in pitch the voices sit on top of one another.

C5M.18.q: Which setting gives thickness and which gives width?
options: Detune gives thickness, spread gives width
Spread gives thickness, detune gives width
C5M.18.why: Detune makes the voices drift apart in pitch. Spread places them across the speakers.

C5M.18.q: What does the Crowd macro change at the same moment?
options: The detune of both oscillators and A's spread
C5M.18.why: Its three slots thicken both oscillators and widen Osc A together.

C5M.19.q: What makes a held note seem to change vowel?
options: Moving the band that is emphasised
C5M.19.why: A voice changes vowel by moving its emphasised bands, and a moving peak does the same.

C5M.19.q: Why does the note keep its weight and top as the band moves?
options: Peak lifts a band and removes nothing
C5M.19.why: Peak leaves everything outside the lifted band as it was.

C5M.19.q: What is the second slot on the Talk macro for?
options: Making the band taller as it rises
C5M.19.why: It raises the resonance, which on Peak is the height of the band.

C5M.20.q: Where does the Steps warp roughen the sound?
options: In the oscillator's wave, so it follows the pitch
C5M.20.why: Steps cuts each cycle into flat steps, so the roughness moves with the note.

options: Rounds the finished signal's level to a coarse grid
C5M.20.why: Crush works on the finished signal, whatever note is playing.

C5M.20.q: What does the Bits macro show a macro can do?
options: Reach into the oscillator and the effects at once
C5M.20.why: One slot goes to the warp amount and the other to the distortion's drive.

C5M.21.q: What does folding do to a sine?
C5M.21.why: A sine has one harmonic, and each fold adds more.

C5M.21.q: Why does growing fold sound metallic?
options: The harmonics rise and fall unevenly
C5M.21.why: The new harmonics do not grow steadily. They shift in an uneven way as the amount rises.

C5M.21.q: Why does the second slot lower the filter as folding rises?
options: To hold back the shrill top
C5M.21.why: Heavy folding gets shrill, so the filter moves the other way to keep the top under control.

C6.6.q: What does Fold do to a wave?
options: Turns it up and folds back what passes the top
C6.6.why: Fold works on the wave's height: whatever passes the top is folded back down.

C6.6.q: As the Fold amount rises, how do the harmonics behave?
C6.6.why: The bars rise and fall in turn, which is why folding sounds metallic.

C6.6.q: With Steps, what happens as the number of steps in a cycle gets smaller?
C6.6.why: Fewer steps make a coarser staircase, and a rougher tone.

C6.6.q: Flip at half way on a sine makes the note seem to do what?
C6.6.why: With the second half turned over, the wave repeats twice as often.

C1.11.q: What does phase distortion do to a sine?
options: Reads it at an uneven speed
C1.11.why: The sine is hurried through part of the cycle and slowed through the rest, which bends its shape.

C1.11.q: As the reading gets more uneven, what happens to the tone?
C1.11.why: A more bent wave has more harmonics, so it sounds brighter, with no filter involved.

C1.11.q: How did the recorded analogue saw differ from the textbook saw?
options: It was rounder, and rounder still on high notes
C1.11.why: The measured saw had a rounded corner, more so as the notes got higher.

C1.11.q: In the Phase pulse and Formant tables, what does Position choose?
options: How narrow the pulse is, or where the band sits
C1.11.why: Position is where along the table you are: a narrower pulse, or a higher band.

CT.7.q: What two things make up a snare-like hit?
options: A short tone and a burst of noise
CT.7.why: The tone gives a body and a rough pitch; the noise gives the crack.

CT.7.q: Which part gives the hit its crack?
CT.7.why: Noise fills the spectrum right across, which is heard as the crack on top.

CT.7.q: You want the hit tight and dry. What do you change?
CT.7.why: Both parts share one envelope, and a short decay cuts them off quickly.

CT.8.q: Where does most of a boom's size come from?
CT.8.why: A boom is low and is allowed to ring for seconds; lasting is what makes it seem large.

CT.8.q: Why add a little distortion to a boom?
options: To add harmonics so it is heard as well as felt
CT.8.why: The added harmonics sit where every speaker can play them.

CT.8.q: What does the room after the boom do?
options: Carries the sound on after the note fades
CT.8.why: The reverb keeps the boom going once the note itself has gone.

CT.8.q: What does the small fall in pitch at the front add?
options: A push at the very start
CT.8.why: As on the kick, a quick fall in pitch gives the front of the hit a knock.

CT.9.q: What does a fast envelope on the filter do to a bass note?
options: Puts a bright front on it
CT.9.why: The filter opens for an instant at the start, then the note settles to its dull body.

CT.9.q: The filter envelope's decay is made much longer. What does the snap become?
CT.9.why: A very short decay is a snap; a long one lets the brightness arrive and leave at leisure.

CT.9.q: What does raising resonance do to the snap?
CT.9.why: The resonant peak is swept across the note's harmonics in an instant.

CT.10.q: Why does a pure low sine vanish on small speakers?
options: Its single harmonic is too low for them to reproduce
CT.10.why: A sine has one harmonic, and a very low one is below what small speakers can play.

CT.10.q: How does distortion make a sub audible everywhere?
options: It raises the note an octave
It adds harmonics above the low one
CT.10.why: The new harmonics sit at two, three, four times the frequency, where any speaker can play them.

CT.10.q: What is the EQ after the distortion for?
options: Turning down the fizz at the top
CT.10.why: It tames the highest added harmonics and leaves the middle ones that carry the note.

CT.10.q: What does lowering the distortion's Mix give you?
options: The clean sub with some edge laid over it
CT.10.why: Mix blends the clean signal back in, so the weight stays and the edge is added.

CT.11.q: What is a riser made from in this lesson?
options: An envelope with a long attack sent to pitch
CT.11.why: The long attack is a slow ramp, and sending it to pitch makes the note climb.

CT.11.q: How do you make the riser brighten as it climbs?
options: Send the same envelope to the filter as well
CT.11.why: One envelope can lift pitch and cutoff together through a matrix row.

CT.11.q: You want a longer build. What do you change?
CT.11.why: The attack time is how long the ramp takes, so it is the length of the build.
